title: Which of four similar lengths is the smallest?
description: Four lengths that use the same digits are changed to counts of tenths and put in order. Two of them turn out to be the same length. Keeko doubts the pair and thinks forty one tenths is longer than four and one tenth.
teaching_notes: One idea: a mixed number and a count of tenths can be the same length, and a count of tenths shows it. Watch for students who say a count of tenths is longer because its top number looks bigger.

source: Arrange these lengths in increasing order: 4 1/10, 4/10, 41/10 and 41 1/10.
video_script.why: The child has ordered eight tenth numbers and now meets four lengths that use the same digits in different places.
video_script.substitution: Change every length to a count of tenths, then put the counts in order and match equal counts.
video_script.anchor: Four lengths written with the same digits, drawn as bars cut into tenths
video_script.wrong_answer: forty one tenths is longer than four and one tenth
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says 41/10 is longer than 4 1/10 because 41 looks bigger than 4, but both are 41 tenths, so they are the same length.
video_script.payoff_line: The smallest is four tenths, and the biggest is forty one and one tenth

final_answer.spoken: four tenths first, then four and one tenth and forty one tenths, which are equal, then forty one and one tenth

maths_rules: So 4/10 is the smallest, 4 1/10 and 41/10 are equal, and 41 1/10 is the biggest.
Slip: 41/10 looks longer than 4 1/10, but both are 41 tenths.
video_script.design: One idea: a count of tenths shows which lengths are equal and which are bigger. Assumes the child can change units and tenths to a count of tenths. Wrong idea: the number with the bigger-looking top number is longer. The four bars stay all video.
